Śivadharmapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
It is an upapurāṇa included in the list of eighteen उपपुराणस्. It has been called a śāstra (scriptural treatise) by the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa thereby getting some status of importance.
It is a short work of twelve chapters in which Nandikeśvara reports to Sanatkumāra what शिव had taught to पार्वती and सुब्रह्मण्य. It is a pro-Vedic पाशुपत work assigned to the period A. D. 200-500.
The topics dealt with are, briefly, as follows: origin and worship of the शिवलिङ्ग; construction of शिव temples; offer of triśulas (tridents) and other things to him; giving gifts to please him; ड़स्तिन्ग् on days dear to him; duties of his worshippers and so on.
It is critical of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् but praises various acts of service to शिव.
Several dharmaśāstra writers like देवण्णभट्ट (12th century A. D.) and हेमाद्रि (13th century A. D.) quote from this upapurāṇa.

Śivānanda, Svāmi
(A. D. 1887-1963)
------------------------------------------
A well-known saintly figure of modern India, Svāmi Śivānanda—known as Kuppusvāmi in his premonastic days—was born at Pattamaḍai in Tamil Nadu in A. D. 1887. His parents were Veṅgu Ayyar and पार्वती Ammāḷ.
After getting the medical degree, he worked as a doctor in the rubber plantations of Malaya for ten years, earning a good name.
His deeply religious bent of मिन्द् made him return to India seeking spiritual enlightenment. He took सṁन्यास (monastic vows) in A. D. 1924 from Svāmi Viśvānanda सरस्वती of Hrishikesh (or Rishikesh) and was named Svāmi Śivānanda सरस्वती.
After a hectic tour of India he returned to Hrishikesh and settled down there itself, establishing a monastery under the name The Divine Life Society. Being an expert in योग and आयुर्वेद, he started allied institutions to teach them also.
The Divine Life Society has branches all over India and outside also.
He was a prolific writer on Vedānta and other subjects connected with religion and philosophy.
He has left numerous disciples who are carrying on his work even now.

Śivānubhava-maṇṭapa
(‘religious होउसे of experience [of God] as शिव’)
------------------------------------------
See BASAVEŚVARA.

Śiva
(‘the auspicious one’)
------------------------------------------
Śiva is the last deity of the Hindu Trinity. He is responsible for the dissolution of the universe. He is the embodiment of तमस्, the centrifugal inertia, the tendency towards dispersion and annihilation.
Literally, शिव is one in whom the Universe ‘sleeps’ after destruction, till the next cycle of च्रेअतिओन्.
All that is born, must die. All that is produced, must disintegrate and be destroyed. This is an inviolable law. The principle that brings about this disintegration, the power behind this destruction, is शिव.
Śiva is much more than that. Disintegration of the universe ends in the ultimate thinning out, into a boundless void. This boundless void, the substratum of all existence, from which springs out again and again this apparently limitless universe, is शिव. So, though शिव is described as responsible for destruction, he is equally responsible for च्रेअतिओन् and existence. In this sense, ब्रह्मा and विष्णु are also शिव. It is perhaps this identity that is revealed by some of the stories in the पुराणस्. If one story makes शिव speak from the womb of the infinite pillar of fire to ब्रह्मा and विष्णु that they are his own aspects, other stories make शिव as being born from the brows of an angry विष्णु or from ब्रह्मा who was intensely desiring to beget a son.
Though शिव is often called रुद्र, especially in his terrific aspect, whether the two are identical or not has been a subject of discussion and even controversy. Some scholars are inclined to think that the रुद्र of the वेदस् and the शिव of the पुराणस् and आगमस् are two different deities fused into one at a later date as cultural integration of the two races accepting them progressed. According to these scholars शिव the pacific deity is a non-Āryan god, ‘more ancient’ than the Vedic रुद्र. Though the ‘Āryan conquerors’ despised and derided the Śaivas and their शिव (apparently because of some of their mysterious rituals and practices), as the two races had to live together, rapprochement and consequent cultural reconciliation became inevitable.
Whatever may be the conjecture behind these statements they are irrelevant to our study here, since we are more interested in discovering the significance of the symbology concerned, to enrich our lives.
Śiva is worshipped both in the anthropomorphic aspect and as the लिङ्ग, the latter being the rule whereas the former is an exception. The most common of his pictures and images shows him as a very handsome youth, white as camphor. His limbs besmeared with ashes are strong and smooth. He has three eyes—the third eye being on the forehead between the eyebrows—and four arms, two of the arms holding the त्रिशूल (trident) and डमरु (drum) while the other two are in the abhaya (protection-giving) and varada (boon-giving) mudrās (poses). He has a crown of long matted hair from which flows the river गङ्गा. He also wears the crescent मोओन् as a diadem. A tiger-skin and an elephant-skin adorn his body as his garments. There are serpents all over his body forming the necklace, the girdle, the यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread) as also arm-bracelets. There is also a garland of skulls round his blue neck.
Man, being what he is, cannot help superimposing his own states on his gods too! Therefore it is but natural for him to conceive of शिव as a man with family. पार्वती is his consort. गणेश and कुमार (the latter also known as स्कन्द or सुब्रह्मण्य) are his sons.
Then there is the large retinue forming a veritable zoo as it were! नन्दि his vehicle bull, Bhṛṅgi the ṛṣi with three legs and three arms, the mouse of गणेश, the peacock of कुमार as also a host of ghosts, goblins and imps constantly capering round him—form his large retinue.
Though he has his headquarters in the icy mountains, the हिमालयस्, he is fond of roaming the earth, especially the बुरिअल् grounds and च्रेमतिओन् sites. All this is in perfect consonance with his nature as the Lord of destruction and dissolution.
Before embarking upon the explanation of all this, which is obviously symbolical, it is better to summarise first the various stories about शिव recounted in our mythological literature:
Once पार्वती, in a playful mood, closed his two eyes, and lo! the entire world was plunged into darkness. To save the worlds from this predicament, शिव willed a third eye in between his eyebrows, sending forth light, fire and heat. Later on, he opened this third eye—normally kept closed out of infinite mercy for humanity—to burn up Kāmadeva, the lord of lust.
When the celestial river गङ्गा, which was descending from the हेअवेन् to this earth, fell ferociously on शिव’s head out of pride, he just got her locked up there! Only after much prayer and supplication by भगीरथ (who was responsible for bringing the celestial river down to this earth) and due apologies by गङ्गा, did he allow her to stream out.
When the क्षीरसमुद्र, the ocean of milk, was being churned, one of the objects to rise was the cool crescent मोओन्. शिव seized it and made it his diadem. When the deadly poison हालाहल also rose and started destroying the worlds with its leaping tongues of fire, शिव gathered it on to his palm and drank it, thus saving the worlds. पार्वती, getting alarmed about the safety of her spouse, pressed his throat so that the poison could not go down into the stomach! It thus remained in his throat, lending its blue colour permanently to it.
Being angered by शिव whose extraordinary beauty had attracted their wives, the Ṛṣis of Dārukavana tried to kill him through sorcerous rituals. Out of the sacrificial fire rose a tiger, a deer and a red-hot iron. शिव killed the tiger and wore its skin, caught hold of the deer with his left hand (which has remained there ever since) and made the iron one of this weapons.
Other stories relate to his destroying the sacrifice of दक्ष, his cutting off of one of the five heads of ब्रह्मा for having spoken disrespectfully, his destroying the three cities built by the demon Tripurāsura, his killing the elephant demon गजासुर and wearing his hide, his having granted to अर्जुन as a boon the weapon Pāśupatāstra, his having become Ardhanārīśvara to dispel the इग्नोरन्चे of his devotee Bhṛṅgi, his appearing as a pillar of fire to teach a lesson to ब्रह्मा and विष्णु, his vanquishing यम, the god of death, to save his votary मार्कण्डेय, and so on.
An attempt can now be made to unravel this mysterious symbology of the शिव-picture. शिव is snow-white in colour, which matches wonderfully with that of his abode, the हिमालयस्. White stands for light that dispels darkness, knowledge that dispels इग्नोरन्चे. He is the very personification of cosmic चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. It may appear strange that शिव who represents तमस् (the force of darkness and destruction) is pictured as white, whereas विष्णु who represents सत्त्व (the force of light and enlightenment) is pictured as dark! There is nothing strange in this since the opposing Guṇas are inseparable. Hence शिव is white outside and dark inside whereas विष्णु is the reverse of it.
The three eyes of शिव represent the sun, the मोओन् and the fire, the three sources of light, life and heat. The third eye can also indicate the eye of knowledge and wisdom and hence his omniscience.
If the sun and the मोओन् form his two eyes as it were, then the whole sky including the powerful wind blowing in it, forms his hair. That is why he is called Vyomakeśa (one who has the sky or space as his hair).
Tiger is a ferocious animal that mercilessly devours its hapless victims. Desire, which consumes human beings, without ever being satiated, can be compared to a tiger. That शिव has killed the tiger and wears its skin as his apparel shows his complete mastery over desire.
The elephant being a powerful animal, wearing its skin implies that शिव has completely subjugated all animal impulses.
The garland of skulls (muṇḍamālā) that he wears and the ashes of the funeral pyre with which he has besmeared his body indicate that he is the lord of destruction. The garland of skulls also represents the revolution of ages and successive appearance and disappearance of the human races.
Śiva is the lord of योग and yogis. He is often shown as sitting in deep meditation immersed in the enjoyment of the bliss of his own self. The water of the river गङ्गा represents this. Or it can represent ज्ञान, knowledge. Since गङ्गा is highly adored as a great purifying agent, it goes without saying that he whom it adorns, is the very personification of purifying or redeeming power.
The crescent मोओन् stands for time, since measurement of time as days or months depends upon the waxing and waning of the मोओन्. By wearing it as a diadem, शिव is showing us that even the all-powerful time is only an ornament for him!
And then, the snakes. The venomous cobras which symbolise death for us adorn his frame in all possible manner embellishing it further. He alone, to whom symbol of death is a decoration, can gulp down the deadly poison हालाहल to save the worlds. All this points to one thing: He is Mṛtyuñjaya, the conqueror of death! Coiled serpents may also represent cycles of time in the macrocosm and the basic energy—akin to sexual energy—of living beings in the microcosm. So, शिव is the master of time and energy.
Iconographically शिव may have two, three, four, eight, ten or even thirty-two hands. Some of the various objects shown in these hands are: त्रिशूल (trident), चक्र (discus), परशु (battle axe), डमरु (drum), अक्षमाला (rosary), mṛga (deer), पाश (noose), दण्ड (staff), पिनाक or अजगव (bow), khaṭvāṇga (magic wand), पाशुपत (spear), पद्म (lotus), कपाल (skull-cup), दर्पण (mirror), खड्ग (sword) and so on. It is rather difficult to find a meaning for everyone of these items. However an attempt will be made to explain some of them.
The त्रिशूल (trident) being an important weapon of offence and defence, indicates that शिव is the supreme ruler. Philosophically it can stand for the three guṇas or the three processes of च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and dissolution. Hence शिव the wielder of the trident is the master of the guṇas and from him proceed the cosmic processes.
It is said that while dancing the tāṇḍavanṛtya, शिव sounded his डमरु (small drum) fourteen times, thereby producing sounds like a-i-uṇ, r-lṛ-k and so on, which are now known as the Māheśvara-sūtras, the fourteen basic formulae containing all of the alphabet arranged in the most ingenious manner, facilitating innumerable grammatical processes. Hence the डमरु represents the alphabet, grammar (the science of language) or language itself. In other words it stands for all words—spoken or written or other-wise expressed—and hence for the entire gamut of all arts and sciences, sacred and secular. It also represents sound as such, the logos, from which the entire च्रेअतिओन् has proceeded. By holding it in his hand, शिव is demonstrating the fact that the entire च्रेअतिओन्, including its various arts and sciences, has proceeded out of his will, his play.
If the अक्षमाला (rosary) shows that he is the master of spiritual sciences, the खट्वाङ्ग (magic wand with a skull fixed at one end) shows that he is an adept in occult sciences too. The कपाल (skull-cup) with which he drinks blood, is another symbol that points to his all-destroying power. The दर्पण (mirror) indicates that the entire च्रेअतिओन् is just a reflection of his cosmic form.
The icon of शिव is never worshipped as the mūlamūrti (original, installed in the sanctum sanctorum), but only as an उत्सवमूर्ति (the icon used during festivals for taking out in a procession).
ŚIVALIṄGA
As regards the लिङ्ग, the emblem of शिव universally venerated, some explanation is needed. Literally शिव means auspiciousness and लिङ्ग means a sign or symbol. Hence the ‘Śivaliṅga’ is just a symbol of the great God of the universe (‘Mahādeva’) who is all-auspiciousness. As already explained, ‘Śiva’ means the one in whom the whole च्रेअतिओन् sleeps after dissolution. ‘Liṅga’ also means the same thing—aplace where created objects get dissolved during the disintegration of the created universe. Since, according to हिन्दुइस्म्, it is the same God that creates, sustains and destroys the universe, the शिवलिङ्ग represents symbolically God Himself.
Whether the शिवलिङ्ग is a phallic emblem or not, is a moot point. Phallic cults have existed in all countries and in all civilizations. It is quite likely that the phallic cults of an aboriginal civilization were absorbed into हिन्दुइस्म् and the worship itself was elevated to honour the ड़थेर्-मोथेर्-Principle of च्रेअतिओन्. This is one view. That it is a remnant of the Vedic yūpastambha, to which sacrificial victims used to be tied, is another view. According to this view, the Hindu temple is a metamorphosis of the Vedic yāgaśālā (sacrificial shed). That it is an imitation of the Buddhist stūpa is another guess that is sometimes hazarded but not substantiated, since Śivaliṅgas have been found even in the pre-Buddhistic civilization of हरप्प and Mohenjo Daro.
Since God is beyond name and form, and since we cannot conceive of an abstract principle like Him, without the aid of concrete symbols, a rounded surface is perhaps the nearest approach to him.
Śivaliṅgas may be cala (movable) or acala (immovable). The cala-liṅgas may be kept in the shrine of one’s own home for worship or prepared temporarily with materials like clay or dough etc., for worship and dispensed with after the worship or worn on the body as इष्टलिङ्ग as the Vīraśaivas do. The acala-liṅgas are those installed in temples. They are usually made of stone and have three parts. The lowest part which is square, is called ब्रह्मभाग and represents ब्रह्मा, the creator. The middle part which is octagonal, is called विष्णु-bhāga and represents विष्णु, the sustainer. These two parts are embedded inside the pedestal. The रुद्रभाग which is cylindrical and projects outside the pedestal is the one to which worship is offered. Hence it is called पूजाभाग.
The पूजाभाग also contains certain lines technically called ब्रह्मसूत्र, without which the लिङ्ग becomes unfit for worship.
ASPECTS OF LORD ŚIVA
Comparable to the व्यूहस् or emanations of Lord विष्णु, is the पञ्चानन form of Lord शिव. पञ्चानन or the five-faced one, represents the five aspects of शिव vis-a-vis the created universe. The five faces are respectively ईशान, Tatpuruṣa, अघोर, वामदेव and सद्योजात. The face ईशान, turned towards the zenith, represents the highest aspect and is also called सदाशिव. On the physical plane, it represents the power that rules over ether or sky and on the spiritual plane, it is the deity that grants मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. Tatpuruṣa facing east, stands for the power that rules over air and represents the forces of darkness and obscuration on the spiritual plane. अघोर, facing south and ruling over the element fire, stands for the power that absorbs and renovates the universe. वामदेव facing north, ruling over the element water, is responsible for preservation. सद्योजात, facing west represents the power that creates.
Iconographically, these five aspects are shown in different ways.
There are several other aspects in which Lord शिव is depicted or worshipped. They can be broadly divided into the following categories:
Saumya or Anugrahamūrti;
Ugra, Raudra or Saṁhāramūrtis;
Nṛtta or Tāṇḍava mūrti;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
Liṅgodbhava-mūrti;
Bhikṣāṭanamūrti;
Haryardha-mūrti;
Ardhanārīśvaramūrti.
The peaceful form of शिव as also the form showing mercy and grace belong to the first group. The forms showing grace or granting boons to Caṇḍeśa, Nandīśvara, Vighneśvara or रावण belong to this category.
All terrific aspects can be classed under the second group. Kaṅkāla भैरव represents शिव who cut off the fifth head of ब्रह्मा for having reviled him and who had to wander as a beggar for twelve years to get rid of that sin. गजासुर-vadhamūrti represents him as killing the demon Nīla (an associate of Andhakāsura) who had assumed the form of an elephant. Tripurāntakamūrti depicts him as destroying by his arrow, the three cities of iron, silver and gold built on the earth, in air and in हेअवेन् by the three sons of Andhakāsura who had become almost invincible because of these three impregnable shelters. Śarabheśamūrti pictures शिव as a शरभ (an imaginary animal more ferocious than the lion) destroying the नरसिṁह form of विष्णु, a story obviously conceived by the Śaivites to assert the superiority of their Lord over विष्णु! Kālārimūrti portrays him as vanquishing यम, the god of death, who wanted to take away the life of मार्कण्डेय, a great devotee of शिव. Kāmāntakamūrti illustrates him as destroying काम, the god of lust, by the fire emitted through his third eye. Andhakāsuravadhamūrti shows him as vanquishing Andhakāsura and later on, on supplication, conferring on him the commandership of the gaṇas (dwarf attendants). Andhaka became Bhṛṅgīśa.
Lord शिव is a great master of dance. All the 108 modes of dancing known to the treatises on dancing have come from him. It is said that he dances every evening in order to relieve the sufferings of creatures and entertain the gods who gather in कैलास in full strength. (Hence he is called सभापति, the lord of the congregation.)
Only nine modes of dancing are described of which the नटराज aspect is the most well-known. The नटराज icon shows him with four hands and two legs, in the posture of dancing. There is the डमरु (drum) in the upper right hand and fire in the left. The lower right hand is in abhayamudrā (pose of protection) and the left is pointing towards the uplifted left foot. The left foot is resting on the demon Apasmārapuruṣa. The whole image may or may not be surrounded by a circle of blazing fire.
Śiva’s dance indicates a continuous process of च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and destruction. The डमरु represents the principle of शब्द (sound) and hence आकाश (ether), which proceeds immediately from the आत्मन् and is responsible for further च्रेअतिओन् or evolution. Fire represents pralayāgni, the fire that destroys the world at the time of dissolution of the world, and hence symbolises the process of destruction. Thus डमरु and fire represent the continuous cycle of च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and destruction. The other two hands indicate that he who takes refuge at the feet of the Lord will have nothing to fear. The Apasmārapuruṣa (apasmāra = epilepsy) symbolises इग्नोरन्चे which makes us lose our balance and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. He is trampled upon by the Lord for the good of the devotees who take refuge.
Several other dancing postures of शिव like आनन्द-tāṇḍavamūrti, Umā-tāṇḍavamūrti, त्रिपुर-tāṇḍavamūrti, and Ūrdhva-tāṇḍavamūrti are also mentioned in the आगमस्.
Śiva is as great a master of योग and spiritual sciences as he is of मुसिच्, dancing and other arts. As a universal teacher he is called दक्षिणामूर्ति. Since शिव was seated facing south (dakṣiṇa = south) when he taught the sages in a secluded spot on the हिमालयस्, he is called दक्षिणामूर्ति. He has three eyes and four arms and one of the legs is trampling upon the Apasmārapuruṣa. Two of the arms (the front right and the front left) are in jñānamudra and varadamudra poses (showing the imparting of knowledge and bestowing of gifts). The back hands hold the akṣamāla (rosary) and, either fire or serpent. He is the very model of the perfect गुरु. He is surrounded by several ṛṣis eager to learn ātmavidyā (Self-knowledge) from him.
Śiva is said to have appeared as a blazing pillar of fire, of immeasurable size, to destroy the pride of ब्रह्मा and विष्णु. Liṅgodhbavamūrti depicts him as manifesting in the heart of the लिङ्ग. The image has four arms. ब्रह्मा and विष्णु stand on either side adoring him.
The Bhikṣāṭanamūrti shows शिव as a naked भैरव begging his ड़ोओद् in the skull cup. It is almost the same as the Kaṅkālamūrti.
The Haryardhamūrti, also called as हरिहर and शङ्करनारायण, has शिव on the right half and विष्णु on the left. A fusion of these two aspects into one god is an obvious attempt at a happy reconciliation of the warring cults of शिव and विष्णु.
The Ardhanārīśvara (half man and half woman) form which पार्वती as the left half represents the bipolar nature of the created world and hence the need to look upon woman as equal and complementary to man.
MINOR DEITIES ASSOCIATED WITH ŚIVA
There can be no शिव temple without नन्दि, the recumbent bull placed in front of the shrine. नन्दि or Nandikeśvara may be depicted exactly like Śiva—with three eyes and two hands holding the परशु (battle axe) and mṛga (the antelope). But the other two hands are joined together in the añjali pose (obeisance). More commonly he is shown as a bull-faced human being or just as a bull.
The पुराणस् describe him as born out of the right side of विष्णु resembling शिव exactly and given as a son to the sage Sālaṅkāyana who had practised severe austerities. Other versions describe him as the son of the sage Śilāda who got him by the grace of शिव.
Nandikeśvara, also known as Adhikāranandi, is the head of the gaṇas of शिव and also his वाहन (carrier vehicle).
Symbolically, the bull represents the animal instincts, especially the sex, and शिव’s riding on it reflects his absolute mastery over it.
Then comes Bhṛṅgi, the sage, who was singularly devoted to Lord शिव, and was elevated to the retinue of शिव’s abode. The sage was so fanatical in his devotion to शिव that he did not care even for पार्वती, his consort! When पार्वती merged herself into the body of शिव and शिव thus became Ardhanārīśvara, Bhṛṅgi was still so bigoted that he became a Bhṛṅga (= bee) and bored through the centre of the Ardhanārīśvara form to complete his circumambulation! Hence the name Bhṛṅgi. शिव, of course, made him realise his mistake.
Vīrabhadra is another deity associated with शिव. He is the personification of शिव’s anger manifested during दक्ष’s sacrifice because of the contemptuous treatment meted out to him. शिव is said to have created him out of a hair plucked out from his head. वीरभद्र successfully destroyed दक्ष’s sacrifice and humiliated all the gods who had assembled there. He is usually shown with three eyes and four arms holding bow, arrow, sword and mace. He wears a garland of skulls. The face is terrific. Bhadrakālī, his counterpart created by पार्वती, is sometimes shown by his side. शिव temples may have a small shrine dedicated to him, located usually in the south-east.
Next comes चण्डेश्वर, a human devotee raised to the status of a deity by Lord शिव because of his intense devotion. He is a fierce deity holding weapons of war and destruction like the bow, arrow, trident, chisel, noose and so on. Though independent shrines dedicated to him are not uncommon, he is usually installed in every शिव temple in the north-eastern corner, facing south. Devotees believe that he can act as a messenger and mediator interceding with the Lord on behalf of the devotees. Hence supplication before him is a duty of every devotee visiting the शिव temples.
Other attendants of शिव are the gaṇas, also known as pramathagaṇas or bhūtagaṇas (demigods or malignant spirits). If they are not propitiated, they can do harm.

Śivadharmottarapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
Classed among the उपपुराणस्, it is another पाशुपत work with pro-Vedic leanings. It has twelve chapters. It might have been compiled during the period A. D. 700-800.
Cast in the form of a dialogue between स्कन्द (or षण्मुख) and Agasti (same as अगस्त्य) it deals with several topics of शैविस्म् such as duties of worshippers of शिव, दान (giving gifts), imparting knowledge to the devotees of शिव, sins and the sufferings of sinners, पुनर्जन्म (re-birth), practice of Śivayoga leading to the attainment of शिव and so on.
Writers of धर्मशास्त्रस् like अपरार्क (12th century A. D.) and हेमाद्रि (13th century A. D.) have drawn upon the material contained here.

Śivapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् are encyclopaedic in nature. They practically deal with all aspects of Hindu religion, philosophy and culture.
They are generally divided into two groups: the Mahāpurāṇas and the Upa-पुराणस्, Though the former contain eighteen पुराणस् and the latter is also said to have eighteen works, the actual number as discovered now is much more.
The Śivapurāṇa—also called Śiva-mahāpurāṇa and Śaivapurāṇa—is sometimes listed under the first group (in place of Vāyupurāṇa) and sometimes under the second group .
The original purāṇa is said to have had one lakh verses spread over twelve saṁhitās or books. The sage व्यास condensed it to 24,000 verses in seven saṁhitās. They are:
Vidyeśvarasaṁhitā;
Rudrasaṁhitā;
Śatarudrasaṁhitā;
Koṭirudrasaṁhitā;
Umāsaṁhitā;
Kailāsasaṁhitā;
Vāyavīyasaṁhitā.
A very brief synopsis of the contents of this voluminous work may now be attempted here:
1. Vidyeśvarasaṁhitā
It deals mainly with the ritualistic worship of शिव. The topics touched upon are: establishing the शिवलिङ्ग and worshipping it; पिल्ग्रिमगे to sacred places of शिव; exposition of the greatness of the मन्त्र Oṁ namaś-śivāya; on the holiness of रुद्राक्ष beads (Elaeocarpus ganitrus) and भस्म (sacred ash).
2. Rudrasaṁhitā
This is a very big saṁhitā and is divided into five khaṇḍas or sections. They are: Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa; Satīkhaṇḍa; Pārvatī-khaṇḍa; Kumārakhaṇḍa; Yuddhakhaṇḍa.
The Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa describes not only the च्रेअतिओन् of the world but also the methods of worshipping शिव.
The Satīkhaṇḍa describes in detail how Dakṣayajña (sacrifice performed by दक्ष) was destroyed by वीरभद्र, a fierce god created by शिव, since सती (Śiva’s wife) being insulted by दक्ष, had immolated herself in the fire of योग generated in her own body.
Satī is reborn as पार्वती, the daughter of Himavān and Menā. After performing severe austerities she pleases शिव and marries him. This is the gist of the Pārvatīkhaṇḍa.
The Kumārakhaṇḍa, the next, describes the birth of Kumāra—also known by other names such as स्कन्द, कार्त्तिकेय, षण्मुख and Subrahmaṇya—and his exploits, especially the killing of the demon तारकासुर. The story of गणपति also appears at the end.
The last in this saṁhitā is the Yuddhakhaṇḍa. Apart from the well-known episode of Tripuradahana—the burning of the three cities of the demons by Śiva—it deals with the several yuddhas (wars and battles) between शिव, विष्णु and the gods on one side and the असुरस् (demons) Tāraka, Jalandhara, Dambha and Śaṅkhacūḍa on the other.
3. Śatarudrasaṁhitā
This book describes the hundred avatāras or manifestations of शिव. Hence the name Śatarudrasaṁhitā.
Unlike the avatāras of विष्णु, शिव manifests himself directly wherever and whenever necessary and disappears after the task is done.
The avataras dealt with here include the following: the five forms like सद्योजात and वामदेव; the Aṣṭamūrtis (eight forms) such as Śarva, Bhava and रुद्र; other forms like कालभैरव, शरभ, Yajñeśvara, महाकाल and Ekādaśa or eleven Rudras like Kapālī, Śambhu and Vilohita; Vṛṣabha; Avadhūteśvara and किरात.
4. Koṭirudrasaṁhitā
This book deals with the twelve famous Śivaliṅgas known as Dvādaśa-ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस् spread out in places of पिल्ग्रिमगे like काशी, Somanātha, Kedāra and Rāmeśvara. It also contains a long hymn on शिव known as the Śivasahasranāma (Chapter 35, verses 2-131).
There is also a detailed description of how to perform the worship of शिव on the famous Mahāśivarātri day (Chapter 38).
5. Umāsaṁhitā
The subjects dealt with in this section are as follows: a description of various sins and hells; dānas or gifts; some geographical descriptions like those of जम्बूद्वीप and भारतवर्ष (India); embryology; on death; stories of सूर्य, मनु and a few kings of the इक्ष्वाकु race; śrāddha (obsequial rites); story of the देवी in brief (same as in the Devī-māhātmya).
6. Kailāsasaṁhitā
This section gives a detailed description of प्रणव (Oṅkāra), the procedure of taking सṁन्यास, performance of पूजा (ritualistic worship) of शिव, explanations of the महावाक्यस् (See MAHĀVĀKYAS.) and other statements of the उपनिषद्स् as also the after-death ceremonies for a saṁnyāsin who dies.
7. Vāyavīyasaṁhitā
This is divided into two parts, the pūrvabhāga and the uttarabhāga.
Since the deity वायु is an important teacher here, this section gets his name.
The pūrvabhāga deals with the following topics: शिव as the best of gods; च्रेअतिओन् of the world by शिव; destruction of दक्ष’s sacrifice; some details regarding Śaivadharma; story of the sage उपमन्यु.
The topics of the uttarabhāga are: the whole world is a form of शिव; various avatāras of शिव as a teacher of योग (such as Śveta, Sutāra, गौतम, सोम-śarma and Lakulīśvara); importance of the मन्त्र Namaś-śivāya; details of Śivadīkṣā (initiation); daily duties; पूजा of शिवलिङ्ग; details of होम; on ध्यानयोग.
It is thus seen that this purāṇa is a comprehensive work dealing with many aspects of religion and philosophy connected with शिव.

Śivagītā
(‘song of शिव’)
------------------------------------------
The well-known Bhagavadgītā has inspired many a similar work. The Mahā-bhārata, the Bhāgavata and the पुराणस् contain as many as forty such treatises out of which the Śivagītā is also one. Though claimed to be a part of the Padma-purāṇa, most of the printed versions—except the Gauḍīya or Beṅgāli recension—do not contain it.
The Śivagītā as available now has sixteen chapters. It is in the form of a dialogue, first between Śrī राम and the sage अगस्त्य, and later, between Śrī राम and शिव.
The contents may be summarised briefly as follows:
Chapter 1
The guruparamparā (succession of teachers) is described here.
Chapter 2 and 3
Sage अगस्त्य initiates Śrī राम into śivadīkṣā (esoteric methods connected with meditation and worship of शिव).
Chapters 4 to 16 form a dialogue between Śrī राम and शिव. अगस्त्य first comforts Śrī राम who was sorrowing for सीता who had been abducted by रावण by giving him timely philosophical advice and then advises him to propitiate शिव.
Chapters 4 and 5
Śrī राम worships शिव, gets a vision of the empirical universe, how it is created, sustained and withdrawn by शिव and how शिव reveals that रावण and others are already destroyed by their own evil deeds. Śrī राम has only to be निमित्त or proximate cause.
Chapters 6 and 7
Śrī राम questions about the cosmic form of शिव or Umā-महेश्वर. The same is revealed to him.
Chapters 8 and 9
These describe how the living beings are born as also their physiology and psychology.
Chapter 10
This describes the svarūpa or the intrinsic nature of the जीव or the individual सोउल्. When associated with the upādhis (limiting adjuncts) it appears as limited. When shorn of them it is the same as ब्रह्मन्.
Chapter 11
This chapter delineates the well-known arcirādimārga (the path of light) and the dhūmādimārga (the path of smoke) that a जीव has to take after death. The descriptions are the same as given in the उपनिषद्स्.
Chapter 12
According to this chapter, शिव can be worshipped both as the Supreme Deity (Parameśvara) and as the immanent deity (Sarvāntaryāmin).
Chapter 13
Four kinds of मुक्ति like सामीप्य are described here.
Chapter 14
The पञ्चकोशस् (five sheaths) and the आत्मन् being separate from them—this is the main subject matter here.
Chapter 15
Essentials of भक्ति are the contents of this chapter.
Chapter 16
The qualifications required of an adhikārin (competent aspirant) are described here.

Śivasūtras
------------------------------------------
This is one of the basic works on काश्मीर् शैविस्म्.
Taught by शिव himself to Vasugupta (9th century A. D.) it has 77 sūtras in three sections: Śāmbhavopāya, Śāktopāya and Āṇavopāya.
The first section deals with the methods which utilise चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् itself and are applicable to the highest grades of disciples.
The second section deals with the method of utilising शक्ति or divine energy through नाद or vibration, to lead the qualified disciple out of the world of manifestation into the world of equal Reality.
The third section deals with the method of unfoldment of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. It is similar to the one described in the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.).
See also ŚAIVISM.

Śivaliṅga
(‘emblem of शिव’)
------------------------------------------
Śiva, the third god of the Hindu Trinity, is generally worshipped in the aniconic form of the लिङ्ग. Literally, शिव means auspiciousness and लिङ्ग means an emblem. Hence शिवलिङ्ग means an emblem of auspiciousness.
Since both the words, शिव and लिङ्ग, also mean the Supreme God into whom the whole universe dissolves at the time of प्रलय (or withdrawal of the created world) and ‘sleeps’ in Him till the next cycle of च्रेअतिओन्, शिवलिङ्ग is the symbol for that Supreme God.
Again, since God (the Supreme, as ब्रह्मन्) is nirākāra and nirguṇa (without any particular form or specific qualities) a uniformly rounded surface like the शिवलिङ्ग can be the best visible representation of that God.
Whether the शिवलिङ्ग is the final product of the yūpastambha (Vedic sacrificial post) as the yāgaśālā (Vedic sacri-ficial shed) evolved gradually into the Hindu temple, or is a Hindu replica of the Buddhist stūpa, there is no clinching evidence to prove it. However, it is an undeniable fact that it is an extremely ancient symbol.
Is the शिवलिङ्ग a phallus emblem? The icon of Paraśurāmeśvara at Guḍi-mallam (in the Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh) being an exact replica of the phallus, gives us this impression. The word लिङ्ग (indicating the generative organ of man) seems to confirm it. However there are many Śivaliṅgās—especially of the svayambhū or udbhavamūrti (self-manifested) type—which do not at all resemble the phallus. शिव for instance, is said to have manifested himself as a great altar of gold from which sprang forth a blazing fire (Mahābhārata, Sauptikaparva 17.13, 14), before Aśvatthāma.
Even supposing it does, one may surmise that certain non-Vedic cults wherein phallic worship might have existed—as in many ancient civilizations of the world—were absorbed into the Vedic culture, and the same elevated to represent the ड़थेर्-मोथेर् principle at the cosmic level.
It is interesting to note that the liṅgas have been described as emblems of the देवी, गणपति and नरसिṁह also and worshipped as such. The sculptured images of शिव and पार्वती worshipping a लिङ्ग, in the Kailāsanātha temple of एल्लोर (in the Aurangabad district of Maharashtra) adds some mystery, leading to the supposition that the लिङ्ग may be a very ancient object of reverence, not necessarily considered an emblem of शिव.
As regards the origin of the शिवलिङ्ग, the Liṅgapurāṇa (chapters 17 to 20) states that when विष्णु and ब्रह्मा were puffed up with arrogant pride about their powers, ignoring शिव, he appeared before them as a pillar of fire of infinite length and challenged them to find out the extremities. They failed to do so and had to accept his superiority. This pillar of fire came to be known as लिङ्ग because all creatures merge in it at the time of dissolution (līyate asmin; layaṁ gacchanti).
Liṅgas are broadly divided into two classes: akṛtrima (natural) and kṛtrima (man-made).
The former include the svayambhū liṅgas (naturally emerging out of the earth) and the bāṇaliṅas, made of quartzi-ferous substances and naturally available in certain rivers, mainly the नर्मदा (in Madhyapradesh). These bāṇaliṅgas are of various sizes, shapes and colour. They are considered holy always, not needing the rites of consecration or invocation and so on.
Another way of classifying the liṅgas is as cala (movable) and acala (immovable). The former are the ones that can be kept in one’s home and worshipped. They may also be carried on the body as the Vīraśaivas (or liṅgāyats) do. They do not normally need the customary installation rites, or a permanent abode.
Such cala-liṅgas may be made of several materials such as metals, clay, precious stones or even wood. The metals recommended are gold, silver, copper and bell-metal. Precious stones that may be used are rubies, pearls, corals, topaz, emerald and even diamond.
Liṅgas made of different materials are recommended for worship to fulfil different kinds of desires. For instance, the worship of a pearl-लिङ्ग can result in the elimination of sins. That of topaz can give prosperity.
As for the liṅgas made of wood, the following trees are considered suitable: red-sandalwood, babul, pine, बिल्व and a few others.
Coming to the acala or the immovable liṅgas, they are the ones made of stone and fixed in the sanctums of the temples for worship.
These liñgas are in two pieces: the pedestal (called पीठ or yoni) and the लिङ्ग proper. This लिङ्ग is divided into three parts: the lowest part is square and is called ‘Brahmabhāga’. The middle part is octagonal, represents विष्णु and hence called ‘Viṣṇubhāga’. The topmost part is cylindrical and is called ‘Rudrabhāga’. It is this part that is above the ground level and is worshipped, the other two being below. The ब्रह्मभाग is buried in the ground whereas the विष्णुभाग is encased inside the pedestal.
The topmost part known as the पूजाभाग has certain lines called the ब्रह्मसूत्र, without which the लिङ्ग is considered unfit for worship.
Sometimes the face of शिव is carved on the पूजाभाग. Such a लिङ्ग called ‘Īśvaraliṅga’. If the whole figure is carved, it becomes known as ‘Rudraliṅga’.
There are liṅgas which have the cylindrical part (the पूजाभाग) treated with the design of fluted facets. These are called ‘dhārāliṅgas’. The fluted facets may vary from 5 up to 100.
If the image of शिव is carved on the middle portion of the लिङ्ग, it is called ‘Liṅgodbhavamūrti’.
See also ŚIVA.

Śivadūtī
(‘one who sent शिव as her assistant [for negotiations’])
------------------------------------------
Devī or पार्वती got this name because she sent her husband शिव himself as a dūta (servant or negotiator) to the demon-king Śumbha (vide Devīmāhātmya 8.28) with an ultimatum to retire to the पाताल (nether-world) or face extinction at her hands.
As a form of दुर्गा she is one of the eight योगिनीस् like Brahmāṇi, वैष्णवी and so on.
She has four arms, a large face and big lips. She is tall and has a fierce appearance. She wears a garland of severed heads. Her crown is of matted hair. Snakes are her ornaments. She is draped in a tiger-skin. In her four hands she carries a spear, a discus, a noose and a shield. She stands in the आलीढासन (See ĀLĪḌHĀSANA.) with her feet on a corpse and a jackal. She is surrounded by a pack of wolves.
